newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Schoolgirls' death strengthens Netanyahu's resolve.
newsitem.headline: Schoolgirls' death strengthens Netanyahu's resolve.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says the killing of seven Israeli school girls by a Jordanian soldier only reaffirmed Israel's commitment to tighten its hold on all of Jerusalem despite Arab warnings of violence.

As a mother screamed "I want my daughter back", Netanyahu delivered the main eulogy at the funeral of four of the youngsters shot dead on Thursday during a school outing to a site nicknamed "The Island of Peace" on the Jordanian border.

"If anyone thinks the murder of little girls will bring this people to its knees... or that we will relinquish our birthright, holy land and eternal capital, he does not know the strength that exists in each person standing here around me today and in the entire nation," he said.

Netanyahu's remarks were a clear reference to recent Arab-Israeli tensions over his right-wing government's plan to build 6,500 more homes for Jews in Arab East Jerusalem, which the PLO wants as the capital of a Palestinian state.

The prime minister's office said Netanyahu planned to press ahead with the settlement at Jabal Abu Ghneim, called Har Homa by Israel, next week. Israel, which captured East Jerusalem in the 1967 war, views all of the city as its capital.
Western officials said the shooting would temporarily take the diplomatic heat off Netanyahu, who would be able to point to Arab violence as the greatest threat to peacemaking.
Jordan's King Hussein, who signed a peace treaty with Israel in 1994, said this week Netanyahu's settlement policy was pushing the Middle East "towards an abyss of bloodshed".

After Thursday's attack several Israeli cabinet ministers seized on the monarch's comments as having possibly influenced the Jordanian soldier who sprayed the schoolchildren with automatic weapons fire.

But King Hussein, who cut short a visit to Spain to return to Jordan, rejected the suggestion. The soldier's mother said her son, Ahmed Moussa, was insane. Jordan said he had been arrested and would be prosecuted.
U.S. President Bill Clinton condemned the shooting as "inexcusable and tragic" but said there was no evidence the killings were politically motivated and appealed for calm in the region.

"I cannot offer enough condolences or express enough sorrow to the mothers and fathers of these children who fell today," King Hussein said. "I can only say that I feel a deep sense of shame and anger that this thing should have happened."
He said he had spoken to Netanyahu by telephone and told the prime minister he hoped to visit the girls' families.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat also telephoned Netanyahu to express his condolences.

It was their first direct contact since Arafat angrily rejected Israel's decision a week ago to hand over only a third of the West Bank land the PLO hoped to receive in the first of three pullbacks due to be completed by mid-1998.

Arafat, who had been refusing to take Netanyahu's calls, would be willing to meet the prime minister providing their discussions focused on the settlement issue, the Palestinian leader's aide Marwan Kanafani said.
But tensions with the PLO are still high over Arafat's invitation of Western and Arab envoys to a meeting in Gaza on Saturday which he said he called to help save the peace process.
Israel, saying differences with the Palestinians should be resolved in bilateral contacts, will not atttend.
